problem: Search latency and front-end load were too high for the volume of queries.
title: Twitter replaces its Ruby on Rails search front end with a Java server
context: Twitter search ran on a Rails front end and a MySQL back end that had been replaced earlier by a real-time Lucene-based engine.
decision_made: Replace the Rails front end with Blender, a Java server built on Netty.
action_taken: Launched Blender in April 2011 and said it would remove Ruby on Rails from the search stack entirely.
observed_outcome: Twitter reported 95th-percentile latency falling threefold, from 800 ms to 250 ms, front-end CPU load cut in half and 10 times more requests per machine.
lessons: Moving a hot path to a runtime that suits concurrent request handling can cut latency and cost.
limitations: Figures are from Twitter's own post and the change was one of several, including the earlier back-end switch to Lucene. The result applies to search, not the whole company.

claims.claim_text: Twitter replaced its Ruby on Rails search front end with a Java server called Blender.
Twitter reported 95th-percentile search latency dropping from 800 ms to 250 ms after Blender launched.
